html:
Bad Bunny, Willie Colón, La Vida Bohème and more

For decades, Latin American artists were put in a box. The world decided what “Latin” looked like: palm trees, maracas and sunsets. Success depended on how well you fit that picture, or how far you Americanized yourself. Ricky Martin, Shakira and Marc Anthony all recorded in English to break into America and the rest of the world. Radio and the labels were the gatekeepers: sounds were shaped to fit formats and songs translated for the market.

Then the internet broke the gates open. SoundCloud, YouTube and Spotify let artists reach fans directly–and Bad Bunny is the best proof. In 2016 he was bagging groceries in Vega Baja, Puerto Rico, uploading tracks between shifts. A decade later, DeBÍ TiRAR MáS FOToS became the first Spanish-language Grammy winner for Album of the Year, and he headlined the Super Bowl halftime show entirely in Spanish. As The New York Times podcast “The Daily” put it: “the hegemony of the English language was a fallacy the whole time.”

The covers changed with the music. For DeBÍ TiRAR MáS FOToS, Bad Bunny omitted his face and avoided tired tropical clichés, choosing an iconic conceptual photograph instead. “I want to show the world who I am… and who Puerto Rico is,” he explained. And he did it as an artist, not by bending to the masses. That’s the thread through the covers I picked: 50 years of records from 1970s New York salsa to today, none of which were made to seek outside approval.

They don’t explain what Latin Americans look like—they look like the artists and their music, as they are.

Willie Colón, La Gran Fuga (1970)
Design: Izzy Sanabria

Fania art director Izzy Sanabria turned the cover into a fake FBI wanted poster: Colón’s mugshot warning he was “armed with trombone and considered dangerous.” The posters went up on telephone poles across New York, and the real FBI eventually asked them to drop its name. It’s the blueprint for everything on this list.

Ray Barretto, Indestructible (1973)
Design: Izzy Sanabria / Fania

A salsero borrowing the most American hero there is and wearing him like a Sunday shirt. Decades before “crossover” became a marketing plan, this cover argued that the barrio could claim the mainstream’s icons on its own terms.

Todosantos, Aeropuerto (2005)
Design: Luis Montenegro (Todosantos)

In 2005, flying out of Maiquetía [CCS] felt like a promise. Todosantos were part of that moment. That year, the band told Página/12 the internet let them break free from radio. Later, the country turned upside down, and over 7.7 million Venezuelans left. The same three letters now mean something else: leaving became the norm, and flying back home the dream.

La Vida Bohème, Tierra de Nadie (2025)
Design: Alejandro Beltrán | AI art and concept: Ariana Ignacia | Photo: Jenniffer Carrillo

La Vida Bohème released Tierra de Nadie in Sept. 2025, an album about Venezuela for the ones who stayed and the ones who left. It started with a recurring dream the band shared when it came out: El Ávila erupting over Caracas. Three months later, on January 3, 2026, U.S. strikes sent smoke over Caracas and Maduro was flown out of the country. Six months after that, on June 24, the strongest earthquakes Venezuela had felt in more than a century killed more than 2,000 people. It’s hard to look at that mountain now without seeing what came after.

Helado Negro, Island Universe Story: Selected Works (2016)
Art: Paul Coors

Limited to 1,000 copies by Asthmatic Kitty Records and pressed on clear vinyl with tinsel sealed inside. We get silver threads shed by his tinsel stage creatures, alongside gold, red or rainbow in other copies. The back note says it plainly: hecho en casa, made at home in Brooklyn. It doesn’t explain where he’s from; it shows you what he sees.

Nathy Peluso, GRASA (2024)

What I love is the tension. The room could be a Danish design catalog: white walls, black leather, low furniture and a cobalt carpet doing all the talking. Then Nathy refuses to behave, with three pairs of pants and the red GRASA stamped on top. In Argentina, “grasa” can mean tacky; she says it’s about pleasure, that everything good in life has some grasa in it. A perfectly composed Scandinavian room, made unapologetically Latin.

Bad Bunny, DeBÍ TiRAR MáS FOToS (2025)
Photo: Eric Rojas | Art direction: Bad Bunny

What gets me is that it’s a family photo with the family taken out. The empty seats become the people who aren’t there anymore.

CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, PAPOTA (2025)

What I love is how much they say with a cheap object. A foil balloon is how you celebrate someone at a kids’ party, and here the duo turn themselves into one: the merch of their own fame, muscles included. “Papota” is Argentine slang for someone on steroids, and the EP mocks the pressure to bulk up after their Tiny Desk went viral. It’s a joke about being pumped full of air and how easily that floats away.

Orestes Gómez, No me fui porque quise (2026)
Painting: Guillermo Carrasquero

The motorizado is the guy Caracas fears and admires at the same time, and Guillermo Carrasquero gives him the slow, handmade treatment usually saved for saints and presidents. Stuck in a wheelie the square can barely hold, he’s all bravado and no destination. For an album called No me fui porque quise, made by a musician who spent years away, that feels right: the street you carry with you, frozen mid-trick.

Rawayana, ¿Dónde es el after? (2026)
Art: Joaquin Salim

The album asks the question every night out ends with: Where’s the after? So we made real matchbooks and handed them out, the kind you pocket at 4 a.m. and find in your jeans a week later. The answer is on the striker: a phone number. Call it and find something new.

Joaquin Salim is Head of Creative at MATTE in New York.
